levels.name: Foundation
levels.focus: Complements, doubling, and quick addition and subtraction
levels.outcome: Take any number from 100, 1000 or 10000 instantly. Add and subtract two-digit numbers mentally. Double and halve with confidence.

methods.does: Taking any number away from 100, 1000 or 10000
methods.classroom: All from 9, and the last from 10
methods.applies: Whenever you subtract from a base — 100, 1000, 10000. Every digit except the last comes off 9; the last comes off 10.
methods.notApplies: Not for ordinary subtraction like 47 − 23, where neither number is a base.
methods.mistake: Taking the last digit from 9 as well, giving 642 instead of 643.
methods.guardrail: The number being subtracted must have no more digits than the base, and must not end in 0 at first — trailing zeros need a different handling and confuse a beginner.

methods.does: Finding the complement — what a number needs to reach the next ten or hundred
methods.applies: Any single or two-digit number, finding what it needs to make 10, 100 or 1000.
methods.notApplies: Not needed once a child adds fluently without thinking in complements.
methods.steps:
What does 68 need to make 100?
All from 9, last from 10: 3 and 2 → 32
methods.mistake: Forgetting that a number ending in 0 takes its last digit from 10 as well, so 450 → 550 not 560.
methods.guardrail: Complements are the foundation of everything later. A child should be quick at this before any multiplication method is introduced.

methods.does: Doubling and halving any number
methods.applies: Any number. Doubling repeatedly gives ×4 and ×8; halving gives ÷2, ÷4.
methods.notApplies: Halving an odd number introduces a half, which should wait until decimals.
methods.steps:
Double 47
Double the tens: 80
Double the units: 14
80 + 14 = 94
methods.mistake: Doubling the digits separately and writing 814 instead of carrying.
methods.guardrail: Only give even numbers for halving at this level.

methods.does: Adding and subtracting by completing to a ten
methods.sanskrit: Ekadhikena Purvena (by one more than the one before)
methods.applies: Adding a number close to a ten or hundred — add the round number, then adjust.
methods.notApplies: Not worth it when both numbers are already easy, like 23 + 14.
methods.steps:
68 + 27
Add 30: 98
Take back 3: 95
methods.mistake: Adjusting the wrong way — adding 3 back instead of taking it off.
methods.guardrail: The number added should be within 3 of a ten, or the adjustment is harder than the sum.

levels.name: Multiplication I
levels.focus: The special multiplications that give an answer in one line
levels.outcome: Multiply by 11 and 12 instantly. Square any number ending in 5. Multiply numbers near 100 without long multiplication.

methods.does: Multiplying any number by 11
methods.applies: Any number times 11. Write the first digit, then each pair added, then the last digit.
methods.notApplies: Not for 12 or 13 — those need a different handling.
methods.steps:
35 × 11
First digit 3
3 + 5 = 8
Last digit 5
Answer 385
methods.mistake: Not carrying when a pair adds to more than 9 — 68 × 11 gives 748, not 6148.
methods.guardrail: Start with pairs that do not carry (below 10), then introduce carrying.

methods.does: Squaring any number ending in 5
methods.classroom: One more than the one before
methods.applies: Only numbers ending in 5, being squared. 25², 65², 115².
methods.notApplies: Not for numbers ending in anything else, and not for two different numbers.
methods.steps:
65²
Take the 6, multiply by one more: 6 × 7 = 42
Write 25 after it
Answer 4225
methods.mistake: Using it for 65 × 75, where both end in 5 but they are different numbers.
methods.guardrail: The number must end in 5 AND be multiplied by itself. Never generate a sum where only one condition holds.

methods.does: Multiplying two numbers with the same tens digit whose units add to 10
methods.applies: 43 × 47 — same tens digit, units summing to 10. Also 62 × 68, 91 × 99.
methods.notApplies: If the tens digits differ, or the units do not add to 10.
methods.steps:
43 × 47
Tens digit 4, times one more: 4 × 5 = 20
Units: 3 × 7 = 21
Answer 2021
methods.mistake: Writing the units product as a single digit — 91 × 99 needs 09, not 9.
methods.guardrail: Both conditions must hold exactly. The right-hand part always fills two digits.

methods.does: Multiplying two numbers just below 100
methods.applies: Both numbers close to a base — 100 works best. 97 × 96, 88 × 91.
methods.notApplies: If either number is far from the base, this is more work than long multiplication.
methods.steps:
97 × 96
How far below 100: −3 and −4
Cross-subtract: 97 − 4 = 93
Multiply the differences: 3 × 4 = 12
Answer 9312
methods.mistake: Not padding the right-hand side — 98 × 97 gives 06, so 9506 not 956.
methods.guardrail: Both numbers must be within about 12 of the base. The right-hand part must fill as many digits as the base has zeros.

levels.name: Multiplication II
levels.focus: One method that multiplies anything at all
levels.outcome: Multiply any two two-digit numbers in one line, and choose sensibly between the general method and the special ones.

methods.does: Multiplying any two numbers, whatever they are
methods.applies: Any two numbers of any size. This is the general method that always works.
methods.notApplies: It always applies — but when a special method fits, that one is quicker.
methods.steps:
23 × 41
Units: 3 × 1 = 3
Cross: (2×1) + (3×4) = 14 → write 4, carry 1
Tens: 2 × 4 = 8, plus carry 1 = 9
Answer 943
methods.mistake: Losing a carry from the crosswise step.
methods.guardrail: Introduce with sums that do not carry, then with one carry, then freely.

methods.does: Multiplying near a base that is not a power of ten
methods.applies: Numbers near 50, 200, 250, 500 — a convenient multiple of a power of ten.
methods.notApplies: If no convenient working base is near, use vertically and crosswise.
methods.steps:
48 × 47, working base 50
Differences: −2 and −3
Cross-subtract: 48 − 3 = 45
Multiply by base ratio: 45 × 5 = 225
Differences multiplied: 2 × 3 = 06
Answer 2256
methods.mistake: Forgetting to multiply the left-hand part by the ratio between the working base and the power of ten.
methods.guardrail: Only set sums where both numbers are within about 5 of the working base.

methods.does: Choosing which method fits a sum
methods.applies: Any multiplication. The child looks at the numbers and decides before starting.
methods.steps:
Look at the numbers.
Both near 100? Base method.
Ends in 5 and squared? One more than before.
Same tens, units make 10? That method.
Otherwise vertically and crosswise.
methods.mistake: Reaching for a special method when the numbers do not fit it.
methods.guardrail: This is an exercise type in its own right — a page mixing several shapes, where the child names the method before working it.

levels.name: Squares, cubes and bigger multiplication
levels.focus: Extending the general method, and squaring anything
levels.outcome: Multiply three-digit numbers, square any two-digit number, and cube small numbers.

methods.does: Multiplying three-digit and larger numbers
methods.applies: Any two numbers of three or more digits.
methods.steps: The same crosswise pattern, with more steps: 5 for 3×3.
methods.mistake: Missing one of the crosswise pairs in the middle steps.
methods.guardrail: Only introduce after 2×2 is completely fluent.

methods.does: Squaring any two-digit number
methods.applies: Squaring any number. The duplex of a digit is its square; of two digits, twice their product.
methods.notApplies: For numbers ending in 5, the special method is quicker.
methods.steps:
43²
Duplex of 3 = 9
Duplex of 43 = 2 × 4 × 3 = 24
Duplex of 4 = 16
Assemble: 16 | 24 | 9 → 1849
methods.mistake: Forgetting to double in the middle duplex.
methods.guardrail: Avoid numbers ending in 5, since the earlier method is better there and teaches the wrong instinct here.

methods.does: Squaring a number near a base
methods.applies: Squaring a number close to 100 or 1000. 98², 103².
methods.steps:
98²
Deficiency −2
98 − 2 = 96
Deficiency squared: 04
Answer 9604
methods.mistake: Not padding the right-hand part to the width of the base.
methods.guardrail: Within about 12 of the base.

methods.does: Cubing a two-digit number
methods.applies: Cubing any two-digit number, using a ratio series.
methods.steps:
14³
Ratio 4/1
Series: 1, 4, 16, 64
Double the middle two: 8, 32
Add and carry: 2744
methods.mistake: Doubling the wrong terms in the series.
methods.guardrail: Keep to numbers below 30 at this level.

levels.name: Division
levels.outcome: Divide by numbers near a base, and by any number using the flag method.

methods.does: Dividing by a number just below a base
methods.applies: Divisors just below 10, 100, 1000 — like 8, 9, 88, 97.
methods.notApplies: Divisors above the base, or far from it.
methods.steps:
1234 ÷ 88
Complement of 88 is 12
Bring down and add: quotient 14, remainder 2
methods.mistake: Using the complement wrongly when the divisor is above the base.
methods.guardrail: Divisor must be below the base and within about 12 of it.

methods.does: Dividing by any number using a flag digit
methods.applies: Any divisor. The last digit becomes the flag and the rest divides.
methods.steps:
2695 ÷ 32
Flag the 2, divide by 3
Subtract the cross product at each step
Quotient 84, remainder 7
methods.mistake: Forgetting to subtract the flag product before the next division.
methods.guardrail: Start with two-digit divisors where the first digit divides cleanly.

methods.does: Dividing when the divisor is a transposed expression
methods.applies: Divisors just above a base — 12, 13, 112.
methods.notApplies: Divisors below the base, where Nikhilam is better.
methods.steps:
1234 ÷ 12
Transpose 12 → −2
Bring down, multiply, add
Quotient 102, remainder 10
methods.mistake: Using the wrong sign on the transposed digit.
methods.guardrail: Divisor must be just above the base.

levels.name: Roots, fractions and algebra
levels.focus: The remaining methods, and applying them beyond arithmetic
levels.outcome: Find square and cube roots, work with recurring decimals, and solve simple equations by Vedic methods.

methods.does: Finding the square root of a perfect square
methods.applies: Perfect squares. The last digit and the digit sum narrow it to one answer.
methods.notApplies: Not for numbers that are not perfect squares — that needs the full duplex method.
methods.steps:
√1849
Pairs: 18 | 49
Largest square under 18 is 16, so first digit 4
Last digit 9 means the root ends in 3 or 7
43² = 1849, so 43
methods.mistake: Choosing the wrong ending when both candidates are plausible.
methods.guardrail: Only perfect squares at this level.

methods.does: Finding the cube root of a perfect cube
methods.applies: Perfect cubes up to six digits. The last digit gives the last digit of the root directly.
methods.notApplies: Not for numbers that are not perfect cubes.
methods.steps:
∛12167
Last digit 7 → root ends in 3
First group 12 → between 2³ and 3³, so first digit 2
Answer 23
methods.mistake: Forgetting that the last digits pair up as 2↔8 and 3↔7.
methods.guardrail: Perfect cubes only.

methods.does: Turning a fraction into a recurring decimal
methods.applies: Denominators ending in 9 — 1/19, 1/29 — and by extension those ending in 1, 3, 7.
methods.notApplies: Denominators that give a terminating decimal.
methods.steps:
1/19
One more than 1 is 2
Divide by 2 repeatedly, carrying remainders
0.052631578947368421...
methods.mistake: Losing track of the carried remainder over a long recurrence.
methods.guardrail: Start with 1/19, where the pattern is shortest to follow.

methods.does: Solving a simple equation in one line
methods.applies: Equations of the form (ax + b)/(cx + d) = e, and simple linear equations.
methods.mistake: Changing the sign of only one term when transposing.
methods.guardrail: Only linear equations at this level.

methods.does: Spotting when the answer is zero without working it out
methods.classroom: When the total is the same
methods.applies: When a term is common to both sides, or the totals of numerator and denominator match.
methods.steps:
12x + 3x = 4x + 5x has no common factor to cancel, so check the sums.
Where the sums of both sides are equal, x = 0.
methods.mistake: Applying it where the symmetry is only apparent.
methods.guardrail: This is a recognition exercise, not a calculation one.
